theme: Do you indeed decree what is right?
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 58. It is one of the hardest psalms in the Psalter, a cry for God to judge unjust rulers. Read it as the voice of the oppressed asking for justice, and notice where it ends.
settingTheScene: Psalm 58 is a Miktam of David set to the tune “Do Not Destroy.” It addresses corrupt rulers and judges, the very people Amos condemned for trampling the poor. This is the first of five psalms in this unit about injustice, and the Psalter’s prayer for God to act as judge when human courts fail.
observation: “Do you indeed decree what is right, O gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly?” (v. 1).
“No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth” (v. 2).
“The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies” (v. 3).
“They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear” (vv. 4-5).
“O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD!” (v. 6).
“Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime” (v. 8).
“The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance” (v. 10).
“Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth” (v. 11).
interpretation:
The opening question is directed at those who hold power in the courts, possibly human judges or rulers. They are supposed to “decree what is right,” but their hearts devise wrongs. The scandal is not just that they commit injustice, but that they do it while sitting in judgment. When the institutions designed to protect the weak become tools of the strong, the cry for justice goes up.

The language of the psalm is vivid and violent: teeth broken, fangs torn out, a snail melting. These are not private threats but prayers addressed to God. The psalmist does not take up the sword. He asks God to act. It is important to see this difference. The imprecatory psalms place vengeance in God’s hands. They express honest anger at evil and trust that God will deal with it.

How should Christians read such psalms? We cannot treat them as a license for personal hatred. Jesus taught us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. Yet these psalms still teach us something. They teach that God cares about injustice, that evil is not trivial, and that it is right to want it stopped. They give voice to those who suffer under oppression and who have no other recourse. We can pray them on behalf of the oppressed, and ultimately we can read them in light of the cross, where God’s judgment on evil was carried out in Christ, and at the last day, when it will be completed.

The key line is the last: “Surely there is a God who judges on earth.” It is a statement of faith in the face of apparent injustice. Evil does not have the last word. The psalm teaches us to wait for the God who sees.
connection: Jesus said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6), and told of a widow who pleaded with an unjust judge until God’s justice was shown (Luke 18:1-8). Revelation 6:9-10 shows the souls of martyrs crying, “How long?” Paul says, “Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Acts 17:31 says God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed.
application:
Pray for someone who is suffering under an unjust system, and ask God to act.

Examine your own use of whatever power you have. Are you using it for justice?

Remember that vengeance belongs to God, and trust him with what you cannot fix.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to break the power of the oppressor and defend the weak.
Ask him to keep you from taking vengeance yourself.
Tell him you believe there is a God who judges on earth.
